text: Sir John Shipley Rowlinson FRS FREng (12 May 1926 – 15 August 2018) was a British chemist born in Handforth, Cheshire. He attended the independent Rossall School in Fleetwood and studied chemistry at Trinity College, Oxford, where he received a Millard scholarship in 1944 and graduated with first-class honours in 1948. He completed his D.Phil. in 1950 in chemical kinetics under J. D. Lambert. In 1950, he won a Fulbright scholarship and became a research associate at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, where he worked with C. F. Curtiss on physical chemistry topics under Joseph O. Hirschfelder. In 1951, he moved to the University of Manchester, where he served as a Fellow, lecturer, and senior lecturer. In 1961, he was appointed Professor in Chemical Technology at Imperial College London. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1970 and a Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering in 1976. In 1974, he returned to Oxford as Dr Lee's Professor of Chemistry and retired in 1993, becoming an Emeritus Fellow of Exeter College, Oxford. After retirement, he continued to publish scientific papers. He received the Faraday Lectureship Prize in 1983 for 'exceptional contributions to physical or theoretical chemistry' and was knighted in the 2000 Birthday Honours. In 2008, he was awarded the Sidney M. Edelstein Award for Outstanding Achievement in the History of Chemistry by the American Chemical Society. Throughout his career, he authored more than 200 papers and book chapters, with primary focus on capillarity and cohesion—the forces that make similar molecules stick together. His co-authored work, The Molecular Theory of Capillarity (1982), is widely cited, with over 2,000 citations by 2010, and his earlier book Liquids and Liquid Mixtures (1958) is described as a "classic" by Benjamin Widom. His 2002 book Cohesion provides a detailed account of intermolecular forces, their scientific history, and their impact on matter's properties. He also co-authored Thermodynamics for Chemical Engineers (1975). Other topics included phase transitions, critical phenomena, computer simulations of interfaces, glaciers, and information theory. He wrote extensively on the history of science, beginning with a 1973 Nature paper titled The Legacy of van der Waals, followed by a 1988 translation of van der Waals' doctoral thesis and a 1996 biography of the Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals (1837–1923). His colleague Benjamin Widom praised both the translation and the accompanying introduction as "no less[...] than a masterwork" and "brilliant both as science and as history," respectively. The Molecular Theory of Capillarity also includes a historical treatment of the subject. Rowlinson contributed to the development of physical chemistry research and history of science teaching at Oxford, supported the Museum of the History of Science's collection, and served as editor of the journal Molecular Physics. He was an active member of Exeter College, regularly attending its lunches and alumni events. He was also an avid climber, having climbed the Swiss Alps and the Himalayas. He died on 15 August 2018.
